etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from earlier おづおづ (ozuozu), from reduplication of Old Japanese 怖づ (“to be intimidated, to hesitate”) — the Modern Japanese 怖じる.

etymologies.text: 元(げん) (gen, “element”) + 素(そ) (so, “element”). Calque of Dutch hoofdstof.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 元首 (MC ngjwon syuwX, literally “first, prime + head”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 元 (moto, “origin, base”) + 首 (kubi, “neck, head”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 共和 (gjowngH hwa).
The idea of "government without a king" was later adopted by Japanese geographer Mitsukuri Shōgo in reference to the United States, which he dubbed 共和政治州 (Kyōwa-Seiji-Shū, literally “the States with Cooperative and Harmonious Government”); Mitsukuri anecdotally took this suggestion from a Ruist acquaintance who could only think of the aforementioned regency as the sole example of an East Asian government with no monarch. Later Japanese authors used 共和 in a rather indiscriminate way, for anything from commonwealth, to republic, to democracy. The original translation into Chinese of English republican was Chinese 民主 (mínzhǔ), whence Vietnamese dân chủ (“democracy”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 兵(へい) (hei, “soldier”) + 士(し) (shi, “warrior”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 嘘 (uso, “a lie”) + つく (tsuku, “to tell (a lie)”). Literally "lie teller", or "liar".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 害 is a daiyōji replacing 碍.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 年號 /年号 (nen hawᴴ, literally “year + call”). Compare modern Mandarin reading niánhào, Cantonese nin⁴ hou⁶.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Literal reading of 幾多(いくそばく) (ikusobaku).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 心(こころ)得(え)る (kokoroeru, “to know, understand”), from classical verb 心(こころ)得(う) (kokorou, see below).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 心(こころ) (kokoro, “heart”) + 得(う) (u, Classical Japanese form of 得(え)る (eru, “to get”))

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally a compound of 戸 (to, “door”) + 片 (hira, “broad, flat thing”). The hira shifted to bira in Middle Japanese, an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Sino-Japanese compound of 抽(ちゅう) (chū, “to draw, to pull out”) + 籤(せん) (sen, “lots”). 選 is a daiyōji replacing 籤.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese compound 文書 (*miən *shiu). Compare modern Chinese 文書 /文书 (wénshū).
The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. Now the most common reading for this term.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese compound 文書 (*miən *shiu), with rendaku for the 書 character. The sho changes to jo as an instance of rendaku (連濁). Compare modern Chinese 文書 /文书 (wénshū).
The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing. Less common reading in modern Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Archaic alteration of monjo above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 文 (fumi, “writing; a letter, an epistle”) + 書 (kaki, “writing”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 書く kaku, “to write”). The kaki changes to gaki as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 新入(しんにゅう) (shinnyū, “newly-entered”) + 生(せい) (-sei, “student”).
First cited to 1899.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ufa ki/ → /uwaki/
Compound of 上(うわ) (uwa, “over”) + 気(き) (ki, “spirit”). The use of 浮 is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Classical Japanese verb 滅(ほろ)ぶ (horobu).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Listed in one source as possibly a shift from the sazare portion of 細石 (sazareishi, “gravel, pebble”, literally “small + stone”).
* /sazare/ → */zare/ → /zari/ → /d͡ʑari/
However, the first attestation of the zari form is not until 1677, while the jari form is first cited to 1619.
The child sense originates as a jargon term at places such as a theatre, initially in reference to child visitors.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Appears to be a shift from the jari reading.
* /d͡ʑari/ → /zari/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Appears in the earliest texts of the 700s CE, including the Nihon Shoki and the Man'yōshū. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *muna.
Analyzable as むな (muna, “cavity, void, open space”, combining form, spelled variously as 空, 虚, 胸, 棟; cognate with standalone nouns 胸 (mune, “chest”), 棟 (mune, “roof ridge”)) + adjective-forming suffix しい (shii).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 胴 (MC duwngH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese compound 認識 /认识 (nyinᴴ syik, literally “know, recognize; know, remember”). Compare modern Mandarin rènshi, Eastern Min nêng-sék.
